newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish yields seen inching down at Monday tender.
newsitem.headline: Polish yields seen inching down at Monday tender.

text.p: Polish T-bill yields may slip further at Monday's primary auction, but large drops are not expected as the ministry's increased offer and dwindling demand from foreigners will keep yields underpinned, dealers said.
They said however that investor demand should still top Monday's 1.4 billion zloty offer, totalling some two billion zlotys, down from about 2.8 billion at the last tender.

"Yields may ease but they will not fall significantly as foreign investors are reluctant to take up new positions as a growing current account does not bode well for a strong zloty," said Piotr Korcz, dealer at Bank Handlowy SA.
On Tuesday the central bank said Poland's current account gap widened to $1.5 billion and the trade deficit to $3 billion in the first quarter, according to preliminary data.
In all of 1996, Poland registered a $1.4 billion C/A gap and a $8.2 billion trade deficit. @

Dealers said foreign interest in Polish T-bills may be further diminished by Wednesday's two- and five-year fixed bond tender, at which foreigners were expected to buy-up a large portion of the 800 million zloty offer.
The average yield of the benchmark 52-week T-bill on Monday was expected to fall to around 21.33 percent from 21.40 at the last tender, dealers said.

The average yield of the 26-week and 13-week paper was expected to fall to around 21 percent, from 21.42 and 21.30 percent respectively at this week's tender, under pressure from domestic corporate clients.
Dealers said that an increase in obligatory reserves from April 30 would, in coming weeks, cut the market's liquidity and could also lower demand at primary auctions.
"Liquidity is likely to be cut as costs of cash are higher in order to pay for higher reserve requirements," said Krzysztof Kozuchowski, dealer at ING Bank in Warsaw.

The central bank increased required reserves on zloty term deposits by two points to 11 percent and on all foreign currency deposits by one point to five percent. It left zloty call deposits flat at 20 percent.

Dealers said that next week one-day rates would return from Wednesday's close around the 25-percent lombard rate and stabilise between 22-23 percent as cash inflows rejuvenate the strapped market, dealers said.
"After the long weekend rates should slowly return to normal levels as cash inflows help banks balance their reserve levels," said Renata Krajewska, dealer at PKO BP.
Polish financial markets will be closed on Thursday and Friday for the long Labour day holiday weekend.
The zloty was expected to drift sideways around 2.5 percent from the parity rate for most of the week unless foreign investors buy large amounts of T-bills on Monday, dealers said.

"It may hover around 2.5 percent following dollar/mark trends next week unless foreign inflows give the zloty a shot in the arm and propel the unit up above likely intervention levels," said Jaroslaw Dryjski, forex dealer at Bank Slaski SA.
The central bank intervened against the zloty over the last two weeks whenever it firmed past the 2.5 percent resistance.
Dealers said even large foreign entry into fixed bonds on Wednesday did not necessarily mean immediate upward pressure on the zloty because the auction's value date was May 12.
The zloty closed on Wednesday at 2.49 percent from the parity rate, against last Friday's close at 2.47 percent.
-- Warsaw Newsroom +48 22 653 9700
